items.prompt: Explain the FULL writing process when using digital tools. Include what happens at each stage: planning, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing.
items.answer: Planning: Use a graphic organizer (digital or paper) to brainstorm ideas and organize them. Drafting: Open a word processor and type the first draft, focusing on getting ideas down without worrying about perfection. Revising: Re-read the draft and improve content — add details, remove off-topic sentences, reorder paragraphs using copy/paste. Editing: Use spell-check to find misspellings, then read carefully for punctuation and capitalization errors. Publishing: Format the document (add a title, choose a readable font size), then share it — print, post on a class website, email, or add to a digital portfolio.

steps: Each stage has a specific purpose. Digital tools support revising (easy editing) and publishing (digital sharing) especially well.

items.prompt: A student wants to create a CLASS BOOK about community helpers. Five students will each write one chapter. They do not always work at school at the same time. Describe in detail how digital tools would help them complete this project together.
items.answer: The class could create a shared Google Doc with five sections, one per student. Each student can log in from any computer or tablet and write their chapter. They can read each other's chapters for ideas and leave comments. When all chapters are finished, the teacher can compile them into a single document, format it as a book with a title page, and either print copies or post it on the class website so parents and students can read the finished book.

steps: Shared doc: each student writes their section.
Comment feature: give and receive feedback.
Teacher compiles: format as a book.
Publish: print or post online.

items.prompt:
Compare these two ways of publishing a student's story. Which would reach a LARGER audience, and why?

Option A: Print the story and post it on the classroom bulletin board.
Option B: Post the story on the school's public website.
items.answer: Option B would reach a larger audience because anyone with internet access could read it — parents, students from other classes, relatives, and even people from other towns or countries. Option A can only be seen by students and visitors who physically enter the classroom.

steps: Classroom bulletin board: audience limited to classroom visitors.
School website: global audience — anyone with internet access.

items.prompt: A student typed her informative report and her teacher returned it with these digital comments: (1) 'This sentence is off-topic — please delete it.' (2) 'Can you add more detail here?' (3) 'Check the spelling of this word.' Identify which comment requires REVISING and which requires EDITING. Explain.
items.answer: Comment 1 (delete off-topic sentence): Revising — this involves changing the content and focus of the piece. Comment 2 (add more detail): Revising — this involves improving the substance of the writing. Comment 3 (fix spelling): Editing — this involves correcting a mechanical error.

steps: Revising = changes to content, ideas, focus, detail.
Editing = corrections to spelling, grammar, punctuation.

items.prompt: A student says: 'I want my story to look professional when I publish it.' List FOUR digital formatting steps she could take in a word processor before sharing her story.
items.answer: (1) Add a bold, centered title at the top. (2) Choose a clear, readable font (like Times New Roman or Arial) and set the font size to 12 or 14. (3) Use double spacing so the text is easy to read. (4) Add her name and the date below the title. (5) Use paragraph indents or blank lines to separate paragraphs visually.

steps: Formatting steps: title, font choice, font size, spacing, author name, paragraph breaks.

items.prompt: Explain why spell-check is a HELPFUL but INCOMPLETE tool for a Grade 2 writer. Give TWO specific examples of errors it will and will not catch.
items.answer: Spell-check is helpful because it catches clear misspellings like 'recieve' (should be 'receive') or 'frend' (should be 'friend'). It is incomplete because it cannot catch: (1) Homophones used incorrectly, such as writing 'They're going to there house' (should be 'their house') — both words are spelled correctly. (2) Missing punctuation, such as a missing period at the end of a sentence. These errors require a human proofreader.

steps: Spell-check catches: clear misspellings.
Spell-check misses: homophones (correct spelling, wrong word) and punctuation errors.

items.prompt: A student finishes a digital story and her teacher says: 'Now it is time to publish.' The student wants to publish it in THREE different ways to reach different audiences. Name the three ways and identify the audience for each.
items.answer: 1. Print a copy and add it to a class book on the shelf — audience: classmates and classroom visitors. 2. Email it to parents — audience: family members. 3. Post it on the school website — audience: the broader school community and anyone who visits the website.

steps: Different publishing formats reach different audiences: print for the classroom, email for family, website for the broader community.

items.prompt: Describe TWO PROBLEMS that can happen when two students work on the SAME shared digital document and how each problem can be prevented.
items.answer: Problem 1: One student accidentally deletes the other's work. Prevention: each student works on their own assigned section and does not edit their partner's section without asking. Problem 2: Two students type in the same spot at the same time and create confusing or duplicate text. Prevention: agree in advance on who works on which part, or take turns.

steps: Problem 1: accidental deletion — assign separate sections.
Problem 2: editing conflicts — take turns or divide the document clearly.

items.prompt: A student's teacher says: 'Your digital story is ready to publish, but first, think about your AUDIENCE. How will you choose which publishing method to use?' Write a 3-sentence response explaining how audience affects the choice of publishing method.
items.answer: The publishing method you choose depends on who you want to read your story. If you want your classmates to read it, you could post it in your class's shared folder or display it on the class website. If you want your family to enjoy it, emailing it or printing a copy to bring home would be better choices.

steps: Audience = who will read the piece.
Different audiences are reached by different publishing methods.
Match the method to the audience's access and location.

items.prompt: Create a STEP-BY-STEP guide (5 steps) a second-grade student could follow to write, revise, and publish a digital story on a school computer. Make each step clear and specific enough for a 7-year-old to understand.
items.answer: Step 1: Open Google Docs (or the word processing program your teacher uses) and create a new document. Step 2: Type your story from the beginning. Do not stop to fix every mistake — just get your ideas out first. Step 3: Read your story from the beginning. Look for any off-topic sentences to delete and any places where you can add more detail. Step 4: Click 'Tools' and then 'Spelling and grammar' to check for spelling mistakes. Read through one more time to check for missing periods and capital letters. Step 5: Ask your teacher to review it. When your teacher approves, print it or post it to your class website to publish.

steps: 5 steps: open the program, draft, revise, edit/spell-check, publish with teacher approval.

items.prompt: A student typed her story on a computer. She says: 'I do not need to read it again because I already fixed the spelling.' Identify TWO reasons why re-reading is still necessary even after using spell-check.
items.answer: Reason 1: Spell-check does not catch words that are spelled correctly but used in the wrong place (e.g., 'there' instead of 'their'). Reason 2: Spell-check does not fix missing punctuation, grammar errors, or off-topic sentences. Reading the story again lets the student catch problems that spell-check cannot detect.

steps: Spell-check limitation 1: homophones.
Spell-check limitation 2: punctuation and grammar.
Human re-reading is still necessary.

items.prompt: Explain what makes a digital PORTFOLIO different from a single published document. What advantage does a digital portfolio give a student writer?
items.answer: A digital portfolio is a collection of multiple pieces of writing saved together in one digital place (like an online folder or website). A single published document is just one piece. A portfolio advantage: students, teachers, and parents can see a writer's growth over time by comparing earlier and later pieces. It shows progress and a variety of writing types.

steps: Portfolio = collection of multiple works over time.
Advantage: shows growth and variety; a record of the writer's development.

items.prompt: A student wants to COLLABORATE with a partner who speaks a different home language. They both speak English at school. How could a shared digital document help them work together on a writing project?
items.answer: They can both type in the shared document in English. The comment feature lets each student ask questions or suggest changes without deleting the other's work. They can type at different times, so neither partner has to wait for the other. If one student is stronger in English, they can help the other while both contribute ideas.

steps: Shared document benefits for collaboration across language differences: asynchronous work (different times), commenting without deleting, and flexibility for different skill levels.

items.prompt: A student printed her story and it looks messy because all the text is crowded together. What THREE digital formatting changes could she make BEFORE reprinting to make it look more professional?
items.answer: (1) Increase the line spacing to double so there is more space between lines. (2) Increase the font size (from 10 to 12 or 14) so it is easier to read. (3) Add an indent at the beginning of each paragraph (press Tab) or add a blank line between paragraphs to make the structure clear.

steps: Formatting fixes for crowded text: increase line spacing, increase font size, add paragraph indents or blank lines.

items.prompt: Write a 4-sentence paragraph explaining to a student who has never used a computer for writing WHY digital tools are useful at EVERY stage of the writing process (planning, drafting, revising/editing, publishing).
items.answer: Digital tools are useful at every stage of the writing process, from the very beginning to the very end. During planning, you can organize your ideas in a digital graphic organizer or outline without worrying about running out of paper. During drafting and revising, a word processor lets you type quickly, delete and retype without any mess, and use spell-check to catch errors. Finally, when your piece is ready to share, digital tools let you publish it to a class website, email it to your family, or add it to a portfolio so that anyone, anywhere can read and appreciate your work.

steps: Sentence 1: intro claim.
Sentence 2: planning advantage.
Sentence 3: drafting/revising advantage.
Sentence 4: publishing advantage.
